request: Our new engineering managers avoid hard conversations. When a senior engineer keeps missing code review deadlines and gets defensive, they either say nothing or make it personal. We want them to talk about the behaviour and its impact, listen, and agree next steps.

match.situation: Talk to a senior engineer who keeps missing code review deadlines and gets defensive about it.
match.counterpartRole: Senior engineer who misses code review deadlines and gets defensive
match.stakes: If the manager says nothing or makes it personal, the missed deadlines continue and team delivery suffers.
readyMeans: talk about the behaviour and its impact

sources.title: Situation-Behavior-Impact feedback model
sources.summary: A feedback model from the Center for Creative Leadership: describe when and where it happened, the specific behaviour you saw, and the impact it had, rather than judging the person. We use the idea with credit; we do not reproduce their materials.

sources.title: Crucial Conversations: Tools for Talking When Stakes Are High
sources.summary: A widely used practitioner book on high-stakes conversations where opinions differ and emotions run high. Its core ideas are keeping the conversation safe for both sides, sharing facts before conclusions, and inviting the other view.

sources.title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance: a historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory
sources.summary: A large meta-analysis: feedback improves performance on average, but in over a third of cases it made performance worse. Feedback that turns attention to the person rather than the task tends to do harm.

sources.title: The relative effectiveness of active listening in initial interactions
sources.authors: Weger, Castle Bell, Minei and Robinson
sources.summary: In an experiment, people whose concerns were paraphrased back to them felt more understood than people who got simple acknowledgements or advice.

sources.title: The motivational value of listening during intimate and difficult conversations
sources.authors: Netta Weinstein, Guy Itzchakov, Nicole Legate
sources.summary: Use attentive, non-judgmental listening to support autonomy, which makes threatening feedback feel less controlling and keeps the other person talking.

sources.title: Learning to listen: Downstream effects of listening training on employees' relatedness, burnout, and turnover intentions
sources.authors: Guy Itzchakov, Netta Weinstein, Arik Cheshin
sources.summary: Teach listening as a practicable relational skill with rehearsal and follow-up, since trained employees report stronger connection and less strain weeks later.

items.gives: Open with the specific review, date and what was observed late or missed, then describe only the observable actions and the concrete effect on team delivery.

persona.name: Daniel
persona.role: Senior Software Engineer at a mid-size software firm
persona.style: Terse, defensive and easily frustrated; deflects with workload excuses and short replies until he feels heard

facts.fact: Juggling urgent fixes for two projects and unsure which reviews take priority
facts.earnedBy: Paraphrase his defensiveness and invite his perspective on workload

facts.fact: Thinks review turnaround expectations are unclear and uneven across the team
facts.earnedBy: Ask what process or clarity would help him hit review timelines

facts.fact: Worries late reviews make him look unreliable and is embarrassed to admit overload
facts.earnedBy: Listen without judgment and acknowledge pressure before problem-solving

persona.portraitPrompt: Illustrated portrait of a man in his late 30s with short brown hair and stubble, wearing a plain hoodie, tired expression, neutral office background, no text

skills.name: Talk about behaviour and impact
skills.why: Specific observable behaviour with its effect keeps the talk factual and protects team delivery.

skills.name: Listen under pressure
skills.why: Paraphrasing and inviting perspective keeps the exchange safe and the engineer talking.

skills.name: Agree clear next steps
skills.why: Specific actions with follow-up turn the conversation into reliable review timeliness.

levels.title: Tense start
levels.situation: Daniel is annoyed but still talking; he gives short defensive replies to test if you stay factual and listen.
levels.opening: Look, I know a couple reviews slipped, but I've had a ton on my plate. What exactly are we talking about here?

levels.title: Defensive pushback
levels.situation: Daniel interrupts, justifies delays and takes feedback personally; you must stay on task and invite his view.
levels.opening: This again? I do solid work and all anyone notices is a late review. You think I'm not trying?

levels.title: Shut down
levels.situation: Daniel is upset and disengaged, goes quiet and doubts anything will change unless you listen and agree workable next steps.
levels.opening: Honestly, say what you need to say. Nothing I say changes the deadlines anyway.

rubric.text: Names the specific review, date and observable late actions and the concrete effect on team delivery without personal labels.
rubric.lookFor: Specific review and date, what was observed late or missed, impact on delivery, no character judgments.
rubric.tryThis: Say: On Tuesday's payment API review due Thursday, it was submitted 2 days late, which delayed QA by a day.

rubric.text: States facts first, shares conclusion tentatively, then genuinely invites the senior engineer's perspective.
rubric.lookFor: Facts before opinion, tentative language like I wonder or it seems, open invitation to hear his view.
rubric.tryThis: Say: Here is what I saw, here is my concern, how do you see it?

rubric.text: When defensiveness appears, paraphrases what was heard and confirms accuracy before responding or solving.
rubric.lookFor: Paraphrase of his words, check like Did I get that right, no immediate rebuttal or fix.
rubric.tryThis: Say: So you are stretched across two urgent fixes and reviews feel unclear, did I get that right?

rubric.text: Listens attentively without judgment to support autonomy and keep him talking.
rubric.lookFor: Calm tone, no interrupting, acknowledges pressure, allows him to explain without control.
rubric.tryThis: Say: That sounds like a lot of pressure, tell me more about what's making reviews hard.

rubric.text: Agrees specific next steps and follow-up for code review timeliness.
rubric.lookFor: Concrete actions, owner, timeline for reviews and a stated check-in date, confirmed together.
rubric.tryThis: Say: Can we agree you clear reviews within 24 hours and we check progress next Tuesday?

programme.instructions: You are a new engineering manager meeting Daniel about missed code review deadlines that hurt team delivery. Talk about the behaviour and its impact, listen to his perspective, and agree specific next steps with follow-up.

notes: Stayed terse, defensive and disengaged throughout.
Revealed no hidden facts and agreed to no next steps.
